title: The Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk explores the concept of Prajnaparamita, or transcendental wisdom, which emphasizes the importance of direct experience and personal relationship with wisdom. This approach to practice shifts from individual liberation to serving others and helping them awaken to enlightenment, highlighting the interconnectedness of all beings. By embracing this wisdom, one can cultivate a deeper understanding of reality and transform their daily life through generosity, ethics, patience, energy, concentration, and wisdom.
topics: Him to the perfection of wisdom

Maybe something you might think is, am I devoting myself today to a deeper view, deeper than the narrow, self-centered one that I default to?
Am I curious?
Am I open?

So this is a big topic, this topic of wisdom, because it's pointing to something that's hard to talk about, since it's not exactly conceptual.
You know all this, but it's worth repeating and thinking about often: this wisdom is bigger than skills and knowledge.
Beyond all that somehow.
And the word beyond comes up a lot, right?
Prajnaparamita, wisdom beyond wisdom, perfect wisdom.
So Prajnaparamita is kind of like the secret sauce.

The secret sauce of Mahayana Buddhism, the later school of Buddhism, of which we are a part.

So I think it's worth, here's the scholastic bit, taking a little step back to consider some of the ideas and origin of Mahayana Buddhism, which is mostly kind of clouded in history.
It emerged sometime around the beginning of the Common Era, but it wasn't a big split.
This was not like Martin Luther or anything like that.
It's more like a meme or something spreading through the Buddhist world: a trend in understanding, an emerging idea that not everybody thought was great, but a lot of people thought was pretty great.
And the idea was that we could take what we've always done and just turn it a little bit for the benefit of all beings.
The earlier model had the elements that we now associate with Mahayana Buddhism: compassion, emptiness, really big vision.
That was in there.
And the earlier Buddhism had the idea of service, and care for others for sure.
But the emphasis was different.
Earlier Buddhism, the main emphasis was on the individual liberation of the monks and nuns.
And the Buddhist ecosystem supports that: the lay people give donations and help make it possible for serious practice to happen.
And as the monks and nuns awaken, there are these great positive consequences.
Tremendous merits produced, good things happen.
The universe is a better place because our local nun in the hut up there just popped into enlightenment, and that makes everything better.
But it was like the lay system looking towards the monastic system, as I understand it, early Buddhism.
And Mahayana more or less started to turn that around: let's have the monastics look to the lay people.
How can I help?
How can I serve?
But how can I serve not just running around like a crazy person?
How can I serve from the depths of practice?
And how can we all rise up together?
So that's a vast oversimplification.

And one of the reasons it's a big simplification is the way the story tends to be told: there was the Buddha, like 500 BC, something like that, and then there's like 500 years where nothing happened, and that doesn't make any sense, right?
Just think what's happened in our country over the last couple hundred years.
A lot has happened.
So I'm sure there was a lot happening in pre-modern Buddhist India, changes and refinements and new ideas happening all the time.
But somehow they stayed very connected to what the Buddha's original insight and teachings were, partly by recitation, reciting all these teachings all these hundreds of years.
And here I am, maybe you could remember this list of six things.
They would have monastic specialists who would recite a big long book every day, amazing.
We do have this flattened-out idea of history, when of course history has got to be vastly complex.
How could we talk about hundreds or thousands of years in a few words?
Maybe that comes also from our European tradition, that the European Enlightenment kind of did that, right?
It kind of said everything that happened before was the Dark Ages, maybe everything before the Greeks was the Dark Ages and nothing happened but toil and trouble, subservience to the church.
But now thanks to the brilliance of a few Italian men, we know better.
So it's always oversimplified.
It's still worth reflecting on how we got here.
What is this Prajnaparamita and where did it come from?
It emerged from this broad interleavened movement that called itself Mahayana when it called itself anything at all.
Probably mostly later it got called that.

The ideal practitioner shifts from early Buddhism to Mahayana, from the stalwart individual practitioner, the Arhat or the Arhat in training, to the Bodhisattva, the awakening being who awakens with everybody.
I'm going to help everybody get across before I pop off into anything.
I'm sticking around here in the mess, in the muck.
But I want to be here in the muck wisely.
That's the rub here.
That's the key.
That's the secret sauce.
Wisdom in the system is not just item six.

It looks back at all the other five, or is underneath and supports all the other five paramita practices, and shifts them, turns them, transforms them from an endless to-do list to a joyful, liberating activity.
And this is the wisdom of emptiness, the wisdom of really feeling to your core, not any real doubt, about the non-difference of self and other.
This is seeing impermanence as what makes everything precious, right, and amazing.
And not impermanence as a threat, like, "Oh no, all that I love will be soon gone, I'm gonna curl up in bed."
No, that's a little more reason to get out of bed and make breakfast, take care of people as best I can.
It's also, I think, the wisdom, and again, this was in early wisdom too, it's just emphasized, the wisdom of knowing that actually suffering is important.
Suffering is our teacher.
Suffering we can embrace and learn from, and it can help carry us forward in a wiser, more subtle, deeper way to meet the other beings who are suffering.
Suffering is not just something to fix or get rid of.
Of course, we want to be skillful, we're not going to wallow in suffering, but suffering can be relied on to appear.
When it appears, the bodhisattvas are grateful.
"All right, thank you.
I remember more clearly my purpose and my understanding and what's really going on here."
So this idea of transcendental wisdom, of this turning, emerged around the beginning of the common era.
Many of these monastics were pretty scholarly types, living in great monastic universities.
I was reading recently about the great monastic University of Nalanda in North India, which since has been reborn in Colorado, I guess.
I never know what's gonna happen.
Anyway, it was huge, and it was there for thousands of years.
I think at least 10,000 monks lived there, hopefully none's too, I wouldn't be able to find that out.
There were 10,000 practitioners.
The library had hundreds of thousands of scrolls.
It was like its own walled city, actually.

In the 11th or 12th century, somewhere in there, when Turkish and other Muslim invaders started taking over North India, apparently it was so impressive looking, they thought it was a big fortress, so they sacked it right away.
I think they could have noticed once they broke down the gate that, "Oh, it's a school."
But I guess then as now, when we've got our military thing going, we're not very good at restraint.
We still push the button, the detonate button, and Nalanda was completely destroyed.
The ruins are there.
You can see the ruins still, just foundations and stuff.
So anyway, these monastics living in these big universities, getting excited about these transcendental wisdom ideas, started writing, just like we would.
And now Buddhism is part of a literary culture that writes.
It wasn't before.
And so they wrote these vast, long, far-out sutras, lots of them, hundreds of them, and some of them are long, long, long, long things.
This is the Prajnaparamita literature, and we studied bits and pieces of it.
The Heart Sutra is a distillation of that wisdom literature, the Diamond Sutra also.
And now we're looking at this hymn, which is from that very same literature.

It's an interesting literature because it's mostly written as a long conversation, long, long conversations between the Buddha, or sometimes another being who's empowered by the Buddha, and a number of monks, and occasionally some gods pop in, and they're just chewing over these ideas.
There's like a thousand-page-long session of shooting the shit, basically, Mahayana Buddha style.
So they're great and difficult at the same time.
The Buddha doesn't even teach that much in these.
He mostly just responds.
It's very Socratic or something.
A monk asks a question, the Buddha answers a little bit, and [unclear: "Christ"] encouraged the monk to answer the question him or herself.
Sometimes the monk will posit something.

They'll say, "Well, maybe it's like this," and then they'll talk for about three pages, and by then you've long forgotten who's speaking, and then the Buddha comes in and either agrees or disagrees, or asks a question, and the thing starts over again.
So it's a process of successive approximation, like we're trying to get closer and closer to this truth.
It's kind of like this.
No, it's not like that.
It's not like that because it's not not like that.
The logic uses a lot of negation, as we see in the Heart Sutra, so it's confusing.
But it's also wonderful, and we're heirs to this, so it's wonderful to pick it up and appreciate it from time to time.
Even if most of us won't have time in this lifetime to digest the long Sutra on Prajna Paramita, which is a hundred thousand verses long.
Big thick book.
Anyway, the perfection of wisdom hymn that we chant is straight from that literature, so I want to give you a little context this morning of where that came from.
It's actually the opening of the seventh chapter of one of the more famous of these texts, a text called the Asta Sahasrika Prajna Paramita.
Asta Sahasrika is a very fancy-sounding word.
It just means 8,000 lines.
The 8,000 line Prajna Paramita Sutra.
"Line," though, is a translation of a Sanskrit term called sloka, which means a 32-syllable unit of text.
These were also written in very structured text, like sonnets or something.
They're structured.

And the hymn is great because, like I said, while the texts are mostly in the form of dialogue, and in dialogue it's very detailed and a little tangled in your minds, occasionally they'll burst out into song.
They get fired up.
This is an emotional literature too.

The hymn is an example of one of the monks both getting fired up in a devotional, excited way, but also doing what I was describing earlier, making a suggestion to the Buddha, kind of saying maybe it's like this.
Maybe the perfection of wisdom is like this goddess, and this is how she understands it.
So let me read you the actual chapter that our version came from.
This is the section of the Sutra of Prajnaparamita in 8,000 lines, so a couple hundred pages in, or like 150 maybe.
We have a dialogue here between a monk called Shariputra, and yes, this is the same Shariputra who shows up in the Heart Sutra, the same character in these plays.
It's between Shariputra and the Buddha, and a god named Sakya is going to show up too.
So Shariputra and the Buddha have been talking for a long time already, and then Shariputra says, with the translator's way of referring to the Buddha:
*The perfection of wisdom, O Lord, is the accomplishment of the cognition of the all-knowing.
The perfection of wisdom is the state of all knowledge.* The Buddha says, *So it is, Shariputra, as you say.*
That's good, but then Shariputra goes on.
Maybe he's excited that the Buddha validated him in this way, and he makes this presentation.
He says:
*The perfection of wisdom gives light, O Lord.
I pay homage to the perfection of wisdom.
She is worthy of homage.
She is unstained.
The entire world cannot stain her.
She is a source of light, and from everyone in the triple world she removes darkness, and she leads away from the blinding darkness caused by the defilements and by wrong views.
In her we can find shelter.
Most excellent are her works.
She makes us seek the safety of the wings of enlightenment.
She brings light to the blind.
She brings light so that all fear and distress may be forsaken.
She has gained the five eyes, and she shows the path to all beings.
She herself is an organ of vision.
She disperses the gloom and darkness of delusion.
She does nothing about all dharmas.
She guides to the path those who have strayed onto a bad road.
She is identical with all knowledge.
She never produces any dharma because she has forsaken the residues relating to both kinds of coverings, those produced by defilements and those produced by the cognizable.
She does not stop any dharma.*
*Herself unstopped and unproduced is the perfection of wisdom.
She is the mother of the bodhisattvas on account of the emptiness of own mark.
She is the mother of the bodhisattvas, as the donor of the jewel of all the buddha dharma.
She brings about the ten powers of a buddha.
She cannot be crushed.
She protects the unprotected with the help of the four grounds of self-confidence.
She is the antidote to birth and death.
She has a clear knowledge of the own being of all dharmas, for she does not stray away from it.
The perfection of wisdom of the buddhas, the lords, sets in motion the wheel of the dharma.*
I'd read it again, but we might just go to sleep, so I can send you my notes.
You heard a lot of the lines in the hymn in there, with a lot more stuff, right?
Packed in.
These are very packed texts.
I think maybe our version just got cleaned up a little bit, and so we could chant it easier.
And I really have no idea where our version came from.
This chant is not in the official Japanese Soto-shu liturgy book, hymn book.
It's not in the hymn book, so maybe it's a Western Zen innovation to tighten that up a little bit and chant it.
Seems like a good idea. [unclear: "Das Norman"] sometime if he knows.
So Shariputra says that spontaneously, but then he goes on.
He has a question.
He's not at rest yet, and that's true of this literature.
These monks are really pretty brilliant, they have deep understanding, and the Buddha is right there saying, "So it is, Shariputra."
So it is, Tim, yes, yes, so it is.
And they're like, "Well, yeah, but."
So he asks a question of the Buddha after saying all that.
*How should a bodhisattva stand in the perfection of wisdom?
How attend and pay homage to it?
How should a bodhisattva stand in the wisdom of perfection of wisdom?
How should she attend and pay homage to it?*
And the Buddha answers this very simply, without mentioning whether the hymn was any good.
Sometimes he does, sometimes he doesn't.
The Buddha says to this question about how do you stand in it, how do you practice it, right?
That's what he's saying.
Maybe Shariputra's saying, "Okay, so here's a vision of it.

How do I stand in it?"
So the Buddha says, *in every way, the perfection of wisdom should be treated like the teacher himself.* So kind of a process answer.
I can tell you how to stand in it, but you should really treat it as your teacher, as the teacher.
Sorry, I'm going to turn the phone off for these.
I hit the wrong button and hung up on somebody.
So yeah, how do we stand in this?
And then, before Shariputra can say anything else, a god jumps in.
Sakra, the chief of the gods, jumps in and asks a question about where Shariputra's coming from.
The god Sakra says, *where from and for what reason has this question arisen, holy Shariputra?* Why do you ask this question?
And that's kind of interesting.
Remember the gods in this system, this is like the sixth level of the sixth realm.
The gods in Buddhism are happy, blissed out, kind of peaceful beings.
They're attracted to Buddhas, so they kind of float in when the Buddha gives a Dharma talk.
But they're not super bright, and they're not super motivated about practice.
They're just like, hmm.
And so I guess this caught Sakra's attention.
But Shariputra's answer to him is interesting.
So just to kind of reframe this, it's hard to keep it straight in your head, I know.
Shariputra's having this long conversation with the Buddha.
He kind of jumps into song and lays out this vision of Prajnaparamita as a goddess, basically, right?
She knows the own being of all Dharmas, she has the five eyes, she's amazing.
And the Buddha seems to approve that, okay.
But Shariputra still doesn't know how to do it, how do you practice this?
And then the god Sakra says, "Why are you asking that, man?"
Imagine him with a doobie.
And then Shariputra's answer is what I want to unpack a little bit.
Shariputra says:

*My question arose because I heard it said that a Bodhisattva, who, taking hold of by perfection of wisdom and skill and means, transforms into all knowledge the meritorious work founded on jubilation and surpasses the entire meritorious work of giving morality, patience, vigor, and trance of the Bodhisattvas who observe a basis.*
Let me say that again.
He's telling Sakra, "I heard this thing that impressed me."

What I heard was a Bodhisattva who's practicing through perfection of wisdom and skill and means transforms into all knowledge, is enlightened by, transformed into all knowledge, the meritorious work founded on jubilation, joyful work, and surpasses, this is the hinge, surpasses the meritorious work founded on giving, morality, patience, vigor, and trance, five perfections, different words, of the Bodhisattvas who observe a basis.
A basis, so we'll get back to that.
The last part of his statement to Sakra is:
*It is just this perfection of wisdom that directs the five perfections in their ascent, in their ascent on the path of all knowledge.*
So Shariputra is noticing two different approaches, two different big approaches to practice that he's heard about and he's been studying.
One is practice based on Prajnaparamita and skill and means, connected ideas.
The other is practice based on this thing called a basis.
So what's a basis?
A basis is like the opposite of emptiness.
A basis is believing in the solidity of things, the separateness of things, thinking that you are the person that you think you are, believing in a self, self as a basis.
And it gets pretty subtle.
These monks weren't idiots, they spent their whole life practicing.
Sometimes there's dialogues and then the other monk says, "I know there's not a basis to being a person.
No, no, no, we are nothing but the five skandhas, right, we're nothing but these experiences of body and mind and feeling.
I know I'm not a person, but those things are the basis."
And then the Prajnaparamita fans say, "No, no, no, no," this is in the Heart Sutra, right, even those things have no basis, go deeper, go deeper.
It's like Dogen always telling us, study deeper, look deeper, look more deeply.
So that's why Shariputra is interested.

He's heard that something fundamentally changes in the bodhisattva practices of the perfections: being generous, being ethical, having good energy, being patient, right, being concentrated, serving joyfully with lots of energy.
If you do it on the basis of no basis, all right, and that's the kind of language, the basis of no basis.
The Diamond Sutra says, why do bodhisattvas serve beings?
Because they know there are no beings to serve.
That's why they serve beings, right.
So it sounds weird, it sounds sort of crazy, because what do we have to talk about it with?
Just words and concepts.
So that's where the hymn came from.
It's part of this conversation.
What's the true basis, for want of another word?
Then you flip that upside down.
The true basis is no basis.
And "where do you stand?" is a powerful expression that shows up many, many times in the Sutra on a thousand lines.
Where do you stand?
So I'll do one more little section and then I'll shush up and give us some room to discuss all this madness.
Earlier in the Sutra, another monk is there called Subhuti.
And so now Subhuti and Shariputra are having a conversation about this question of where do you stand?
So can you take in a little more?
This is like source material, powerful and hard to keep in our minds.
So Subhuti says to Shariputra and the assembled dignitaries, some of whom are invisible:
*I will teach you how a bodhisattva should stand in perfect wisdom.
Through standing in emptiness should he stand in perfect wisdom, armed with the great armor, protected by the great armor.

The bodhisattva should so develop that he does not take his stand on any of these, not on form, not on feelings, perceptions, impulses, and consciousness, not on eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind,* it's unfamiliar, *not on form, sounds, smells, tastes, touchables, mind, objects, not on eye consciousness, not on mind consciousness, not on the elements, not on earth, water, fire, air, ether, consciousness.*
*Don't take your stand on the pillars of mindfulness, right effort, the roads, the psychic powers, the faculties, the limbs of enlightenment.* This is like all the Buddha stuff.
Don't stand on any of the Buddha stuff.
*Don't stand on the fruits of the stream winner, the once returner, the never returner, or even* [unclear: "our hardship"], *not even on buddhahood.* Yeah, don't stand on anything.
What should you stand on?
He says this:
*He should take his stand on the idea that this is just form, this is just feeling, this is buddhahood.

You should not take a stand on the ideas that form and so on are permanent or impermanent, or that form is suffering or ease, or that form is self or not the self, or that form is lovely or repulsive.
You should take a stand on the notion that the fruits of the holy life derive their dignity from the unconditioned.*
And so Shariputra is having a hard time with this.
What does this all mean?
So Shariputra says:
*Well, nowhere did the Tathagata stand because his mind sought no support.
He stood neither in what is conditioned nor in what is unconditioned, nor did he emerge from them.*
And so Shariputra says, *even so should a bodhisattva stand and train herself.

He should decide that as the Tathagata does not stand anywhere, nor not stand, nor stand apart, nor not stand apart, so will I stand.* So in other words, the short version is that bodhisattvas who practice this deeply see how fluid, how groundless, how incomprehensible, that there's nowhere to stand, there's nowhere to stand.
And instead of that upsetting them or shutting them down, they delight in standing in nowhere to stand.
That's where bodhisattvas stand.
And the point I'm trying to make is that that's not just like an intellectual or a meditative discipline thing.
It also emerges from love.
It also emerges from devotion.
And so thus we have things like a very cryptic, logical text like the Heart Sutra, which has some passion in it.
Avalokiteshvara, the goddess of compassion, is fired up in the Heart Sutra.
She just saw that all skandhas are empty and everything's empty, and that frees her up, it frees everyone up.
There's no fear, there's no obstacles in mind.
So this is a passionate thing when you realize this.
But it's not something we can exactly figure out.
We also have to devote ourselves to the perfection of wisdom, let her into our hearts.
